heading: Work through a real study
exactSourceText: Ladan and colleagues tested whether breast-cancer tissue slices could predict response to chemotherapy given before surgery ([Ladan 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10542784/)). Biopsy cores were cut into thin slices and exposed for 3 days to 5-fluorouracil, doxorubicin and the active form of cyclophosphamide. Each tumor was called sensitive, intermediate or resistant. The comparison was the tumor's size change on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) after four cycles of anthracycline-containing chemotherapy, measured with [Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST)](/wiki/education/concepts/measurement/imaging/response-criteria) but grouped by the study's own cutoffs: "sensitive" meant more than 50% shrinkage, a stricter bar than RECIST's 30% for partial response. Before starting, the team set a target of at least 55% agreement.

heading: What is still uncertain
exactSourceText: Published agreement studies are small and setting-specific: a breast-slice chemotherapy assay matched magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) response in 15 of 20 evaluable patients but never called a tumor resistant ([Ladan 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10542784/)). A pooled review of 17 organoid studies found no randomized trial of organoid-guided treatment ([Wensink 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8042051/)). When colorectal patients were treated with organoid-selected drugs, none of 6 responded ([Ooft 2021](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33887686/)). Agreement is not proof that choosing treatment by the model improves outcomes. A model may also omit a relevant population, change during establishment or use an exposure that does not translate to patients. Computation may fail in a new context. Even a strong clinical prediction may lack evidence that its use improves care. Keep those gaps beside the useful result.
